rows.grounds: states the reason for the figurative treatment
locates rapid clarity in the qualified subject
names the final state of identity with that

items.question: Why is this figurative treatment used and what result does it produce?
premises: The figurative usage has a specific cause and purpose.
Through that usage clarity arises in the qualified substrate.
That clarity leads to abiding in absorption in that reality.
items.inference: Therefore the figurative treatment is purposeful because it produces clarity and culminates in absorption.
uncertainties: The exact referent of dharmiṇī depends on the immediately preceding context.
items.plain_english: This figurative way of speaking has a clear reason and purpose: through it clarity quickly arises in the qualified subject, and that leads to abiding in full absorption in that reality.

rows.grounds: refers to the previously mentioned qualities
identifies the qualities as powers appearing in suitable forms
gives the purpose of the worship

items.question: How are those qualities approached in practice and for what purpose?
premises: The same qualities are called powers.
They appear in various fitting forms.
They are worshipped in those forms to accomplish absorption.
items.inference: Therefore contemplative worship of those powers in suitable forms is undertaken to attain absorption in that reality.
items.plain_english: Those very qualities, called powers, are worshipped in various fitting forms so that one may become fully absorbed in that reality.

rows.grounds: locates the discussion in that context
explains how powers are drawn in by the logic of invocation and proximity

items.question: Which powers can be drawn in and by what principle does this occur?
premises: A power may be unlimited or limited.
Invocation makes a power present in a certain way.
Distance and nearness affect how that presence is drawn in.
items.inference: Therefore either unlimited or limited powers may be drawn in according to the principle of invoked presence and relative proximity.
uncertainties: The technical nuance of dhavatāsattvanyāya is compressed in the compound.
items.plain_english: In that context, an unlimited power or even limited powers may be drawn in, according to the principle by which what is invoked becomes present, and according to nearness or distance.

rows.grounds: draws a consequence from the previous verse
names fullness as a drawn-in attribute
names luminosity as a drawn-in attribute
names consciousness-nature as a drawn-in attribute
names Bhairava-nature as a drawn-in attribute
states that pervasiveness draws in all powers

items.question: What follows from pervasiveness in the drawing in of powers?
premises: Pervasiveness belongs to the invoked reality.
Fullness, luminosity, consciousness, and Bhairava-nature are its attributes.
Because of pervasiveness, all powers can be drawn in.
items.inference: Therefore pervasiveness entails the drawing in of all powers together with fullness, luminosity, consciousness, and Bhairava-nature.
items.plain_english: Because of its pervasiveness, that reality draws in all powers, along with fullness, luminosity, the nature of consciousness, and the state of being Bhairava.

rows.grounds: contrasts Sadashiva and others with the fully pervasive reality
names what they can draw in
limits their drawing-in to the scope of their worship

items.question: How do Sadashiva and other lower principles draw in powers compared with the supreme?
premises: Sadashiva and others lack full upward pervasion.
They operate from a lower position.
Their worship has degrees of nearness and distance.
items.inference: Therefore Sadashiva and others draw in powers only in a limited way, according to the nearness or distance of their worship.
items.plain_english: Sadashiva and the other principles below the highest, lacking full upward pervasion, can draw in powers only to the extent that their worship is near or far.

rows.grounds: refers to the condition just described
connects to the classification of the path
characterizes it as involving conceptual differentiation
locates the teaching in this text
marks what has been taught here
states that it operates through conceptual counterparts

items.question: What kind of path is the Shakta path as described here?
premises: The state described involves differentiated apprehension.
The path taught here is called Shakta.
It proceeds through conceptual counterparts.
items.inference: Therefore the Shakta path, as taught here, is a conceptual course that operates through counterpart distinctions.
items.plain_english: In this condition, the path taught here is called the Shakta path: it is a conceptual course, because it works through distinctions and their counterparts.

rows.grounds: describes one established in the nonconceptual path
specifies the full range of possible paths
refers back to any such path

items.question: What happens when one established in the nonconceptual path enters through any level of reality?
premises: One may be established in the nonconceptual path.
Entry may occur through any path from earth up to Sadashiva.
The result is determined by that nonconceptual establishment.
items.inference: Therefore, for one established in the nonconceptual path, entry through any level from earth to Sadashiva results in becoming Shiva.
items.plain_english: One who is established in the nonconceptual path, by whatever route they enter—from the earth principle up to Sadashiva—through that very route becomes Shiva.

rows.grounds: describes the heart as illumined by the initial flash of that level
names the luminous field of awareness

items.question: Where and how does awareness realize its identity as supreme Shiva?
premises: The heart becomes pure and luminous.
The first flash of a given level shines there.
That opening reveals the nature of awareness.
items.inference: Therefore, in the pure luminous heart, through that very opening, awareness realizes its identity as supreme Shiva.
uncertainties: bhūmyaṃśa may refer to a level or a portion of a level; the verse leaves the scope compact.
items.plain_english: In a pure heart, illumined by the first flash of that level, awareness comes to recognize itself as supreme Shiva through that very opening.

rows.grounds: defines the means as rooted in supreme will
identifies it as a mode of immersion
names the recipients of this teaching

items.question: What is this means called and how is it understood by those close to the teacher?
premises: The means arises from a portion of supreme will-power.
It is known as the Shambhava immersion.
Those close to the good-minded teacher recognize it as such.
items.inference: Therefore this means, rooted in supreme will, is known by the teacher's close disciples as the Shambhava immersion.
items.plain_english: Thus, those who live close to the wise teacher know this good means, which partakes of supreme will-power, as the Shambhava immersion.

rows.grounds: describes the contents as maya-shaped powers

items.question: How is the Shakta mode described in terms of the inner instruments and their contents?
premises: The Shakta mode operates through mind, intellect, thought, and ego-making.
It functions clearly and conceptually.
Its contents, such as will, are in reality maya-shaped.
items.inference: Therefore the Shakta mode is a clear conceptual operation of the inner instruments upon contents that are, in reality, formed of maya.
uncertainties: The exact scope of icchādi is left open by the verse.
items.plain_english: Now the Shakta mode is described: it works clearly through mind, intellect, thought, and ego-making, in a conceptual way, dealing with things like will that are, in reality, made of maya.

items.question: How can the Shakta mode, though based on maya, culminate in the nonconceptual?
premises: The Shakta mode operates through identification, intention, and determination.
It is a means that works within maya.
At its culmination it becomes nonconceptual.
items.inference: Therefore, although the Shakta mode proceeds through maya-based conceptual operations, it culminates in a nonconceptual state.
items.plain_english: The Shakta mode works through identification and through the sequence of intention and determination; even though it is a means based in maya, at its end it becomes nonconceptual.

rows.grounds: specifies the subject as the bound soul
classifies it as Shambhava in a limited sense
explains both its incompleteness and its flowering
describes its full unfolding when the defect is removed

items.question: What is the status of the bound soul's nonconceptual state and when does it fully blossom?
premises: The bound soul can have a nonconceptual state.
That state is called Shambhava but remains incomplete.
Its incompleteness is due to the defect of the limited knower.
items.inference: Therefore the bound soul's nonconceptual state is only an incomplete Shambhava condition, but it blossoms fully when the defect of the limited knower falls away.
items.plain_english: The nonconceptual state that appears in a bound soul is indeed called Shambhava, but it is incomplete because of the defect of the limited knower; when that defect falls away, it blossoms fully.

rows.grounds: locates it in the Shakta mode
identifies the key experience of that level

items.question: What characterizes the conceptual level in the Shakta mode and what limits it?
premises: The Shakta mode includes a conceptual level.
On that level there is awareness of agency.
Even when clear, it remains marked by contraction as explained earlier.
items.inference: Therefore the conceptual level of the Shakta mode is defined by clear awareness of agency, yet it is still limited by contraction.
items.plain_english: Thus, in the Shakta mode there is a conceptual level marked by the awareness of agency; even when that awareness is clear, it still involves contraction, as explained earlier.

rows.grounds: continues the same line of thought
describes the practitioner oriented to dissolving contraction
refers to the same power or level
states its creative capacity when contraction dissolves
names the power as radiant in that state

items.question: What happens to that power when contraction is dissolved?
premises: Contraction can be dissolved.
A practitioner may be intent on dissolving it.
When contraction dissolves, the power manifests freely.
items.inference: Therefore, for one intent on dissolving contraction, that power becomes radiant and brings about the inner appearance of whatever is desired.
items.plain_english: Likewise, for one who is intent on dissolving the whole mass of contraction, that power becomes radiant and can bring about the inner appearance of whatever is desired.

rows.grounds: frames the objection as a question
asks whether conceptual cognition exists in the Anava means
locates the answer in that context
reclassifies it as belonging to another means
states the defining feature of the Anava means here

items.question: Does conceptual cognition belong to the Anava means, and how was that means defined?
premises: An objection asks whether conceptual cognition exists in the Anava means.
The Anava means was defined by absence of utterance.
Conceptual cognition is treated here as belonging to another means.
items.inference: Therefore conceptual cognition does not define the Anava means here, because that means was characterized by the absence of utterance.
uncertainties: The exact scope of uccāra may include mantra, articulation, or overt expression.
items.plain_english: One might ask whether conceptual cognition exists in the Anava means. The answer is that, as defined here, the Anava means is marked by the absence of utterance, so that kind of conceptual operation belongs to another means.

rows.grounds: locates the contrast in the Shakta means
negates their presence there in that defining way
names the dual structure characteristic of the Shakta means
identifies power with the play of difference and nondifference

items.question: What does the term utterance include here, and why does that distinguish the Shakta means?
premises: The word utterance here includes outward-directed operations and related forms.
These do not define the Shakta means in the same way.
The Shakta means is characterized by difference and nondifference, which is the nature of power.
items.inference: Therefore utterance and similar outer operations are not the defining mark of the Shakta means, because that means is constituted by the power-play of difference and nondifference.
uncertainties: bahvantena is terse; the exact range of included operations is inferred from context.
items.plain_english: Here the word utterance covers outward expression and related operations. These are not what define the Shakta means, because the Shakta means is characterized by the play of difference and nondifference, which is the very nature of power.

rows.grounds: introduces the Anu as a defined term
links the Anu to difference and to the Anava means
names the means in this context

items.question: What defines the Anu and the Anava means, and how does that means culminate?
premises: The Anu is marked by clear difference.
The Anava means operates through concept and determination.
At its end it becomes nonconceptual.
items.inference: Therefore the Anava means, rooted in the clear difference of the limited self and operating through conceptual determination, culminates in the nonconceptual.
items.plain_english: The limited self is defined by clear difference, and the Anava means based on that works through conceptual thought and determination; yet at its culmination it becomes nonconceptual.

rows.grounds: lists the lower faculties and the individual
poses the possibility of pervading Shiva
refers to the teaching under question

items.question: How can intellect, mind, ego, and the individual self reach Shiva if they exist below him?
premises: Intellect, mind, ego, and the individual self are lower faculties.
An objection claims lower realities cannot pervade Shiva.
The teaching seems to say they can reach Shiva.
items.inference: Therefore an objection arises: if these faculties exist below Shiva, how can the teaching claim that they reach or pervade him?
items.plain_english: An objection arises: how could intellect, mind, ego, and the individual self pervade Shiva, since they exist below him? How, then, can such a teaching be stated?

items.question: How does the teaching answer the objection that lower faculties cannot reach Shiva?
premises: In reality Shiva alone is the one reality.
Shiva can conceal his own nature.
Even while concealed, he remains self-luminous and can appear in that form.
items.inference: Therefore the lower faculties can appear to reach Shiva because it is Shiva himself who, while self-luminous, conceals and manifests his own nature in that way.
items.plain_english: The answer is that, in reality, it is Shiva alone. Being self-luminous, he conceals his own nature and then appears again in that very form.

rows.grounds: locates the teaching in dualistic texts
states that the point is established there too
identifies the agent as Shiva alone

items.question: Is this view of Shiva's downward manifestation supported in other scriptural traditions?
premises: Dualistic scriptures such as the Matanga discuss this matter.
They explain the manifestation of Shiva who pervades below.
That manifestation is established as Shiva's own light.
items.inference: Therefore even dualistic scriptures acknowledge that the light appearing below is the established manifestation of Shiva himself.
items.plain_english: Even in dualistic scriptures such as the Matanga, this is clearly explained: the light that appears in the lower levels is the established manifestation of Shiva himself, who pervades downward.

rows.grounds: gives the reason for the previous claim
extends the manifestation to lower faculties
states the appearance of the supreme

items.question: Why can the supreme state be said to appear even in intellect and mind?
premises: Shiva's manifestation is established even in lower levels.
Intellect and mind are such lower levels.
The supreme state shines there.
items.inference: Therefore the supreme state can appear even on the level of intellect and mind because it is Shiva's own manifestation that shines there.
items.plain_english: For this reason, the supreme state shines even on the level of intellect and mind.

rows.grounds: refers to the two immersions or means discussed
states that nothing is accomplished otherwise

items.question: What do the two immersions aim at, and what is required for their success?
premises: Both immersions move toward the ocean of the nonconceptual.
Movement toward that goal is not enough by itself.
Firm establishment in that state is required.
items.inference: Therefore both immersions truly lead to the ocean of the nonconceptual, but without firm establishment in it nothing is accomplished.
items.plain_english: Both of these immersions indeed move toward the ocean of the nonconceptual, but without firm establishment in that state, nothing at all is accomplished.

rows.grounds: states that the result in awareness does not differ
draws a conclusion and refers to the teacher's statement
asserts the primacy of conceptual construction in this context
states that this was hinted at

items.question: Do the means differ in their fruit of awareness, and what role does conceptual construction play here?
premises: The fruit in awareness should not be assumed to differ.
The teacher indicated something specific about conceptual construction.
In this context conceptual construction has primacy.
items.inference: Therefore no difference in the fruit of awareness should be posited here, while conceptual construction is indicated as having primacy in this context.
uncertainties: The scope of 'here' (atra) may refer narrowly to the Shakta discussion or more broadly to the present section.
items.plain_english: One should not assume any difference in the fruit of awareness here; rather, it was indicated that conceptual construction has a primary role in this context.

rows.grounds: states the basis of the argument
names the epistemic status in question
locates the claim in a particular doctrine
states that nonconceptual validity is reached through conceptual sequence

items.question: How is the validity of the nonconceptual explained in the view that depends on conceptual construction?
premises: Some declare validity in dependence on conceptual construction.
That view still recognizes the nonconceptual.
The nonconceptual is reached through a sequence of concepts.
items.inference: Therefore, in that view, the nonconceptual has validity insofar as it is obtained through the ordered progression of conceptual constructions.
items.plain_english: Even in the view that makes validity depend on conceptual construction, the nonconceptual is still valid—but its validity is reached through the ordered sequence of those very concepts.
